title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Surgical Release Criteria and Post-Operative Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with carpal tunnel syndrome seen in a Saudi primary health centre, hospital clinic or hand or orthopaedic service: when to refer for surgical release, what to arrange before surgery, the choice between open and endoscopic release, local anaesthesia and simple pain control, wound and hand care afterwards, expected recovery, complications and when to review. Uses a 2024 narrative review of surgical techniques, a prospective open release study, a long-term outcome study, a primary care review and a Saudi prevalence survey, with product labels for medicines. Not for children, acute traumatic median nerve injury, or conservative treatment (see the splinting and injection topic).
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi orthopaedic or hand surgery society guideline for carpal tunnel release was found; the pathway follows international review articles and single-centre studies. The only Saudi source is a Tabuk prevalence survey, which gives no surgical data.

The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guideline and NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries could not be read from this environment, so their formal graded recommendations are not quoted; the Massachusetts surgical guideline page could not be downloaded.

The surgical review is a narrative review without a stated search for harms in every technique; its journal, year and authors were not shown in the extracted text and its technique comparisons come from other studies cited inside it.

The Kanpur study (India) enrolled 50 adults aged 18 to 65 after at least 6 months of failed conservative treatment, used open release under local anaesthesia and followed patients for 6 weeks; it is single-centre, uncontrolled and from outside Saudi Arabia.
The long-term study (Israel, 186 patients, mean follow-up 11 years) used a telephone questionnaire and is cross-sectional; it is cited for outcome only.

No numeric nerve conduction cut-off was found for the decision to operate; the review lists Bland grades and a motor latency over 4.5 ms with absent sensory response as showing better response to surgery, but no local laboratory normal range is given.
The choice between open and endoscopic release is left to the surgeon's experience and patient factors by the review; no local resource or training data were found.

Antibiotic prophylaxis, tourniquet use, adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic and intravenous regional anaesthesia are not described with doses in the sources read, so no regimen is written for them; the lidocaine row gives concentration and label limits only, and the maximum dose table in the label could not be extracted.
Stopping or continuing anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs before hand surgery was not in the sources read and is left to the surgical and anaesthetic team.
Post-operative rehabilitation (orthoses, dressings, exercise, ice) has only minimal and low-quality evidence according to the review; the pathway does not mandate any of them.
Return-to-work time (mean 11.2 days) comes from one Indian cohort and may not apply to heavy manual work in Saudi Arabia; the primary care review advises avoiding a firm grip for 6 weeks.

Paracetamol dosing is taken from a United States over-the-counter label (maximum 6 tablets of 500 mg in 24 hours); ibuprofen from a United States prescribing label (400 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed, not over 3200 mg a day). Saudi labels may differ.
Figures were read by automated extraction of article and label text; spot-check each figure and dose against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: The median nerve is compressed in the carpal tunnel where pressure is raised; normal tunnel pressure is 2 to 10 mmHg and can be up to ten times higher in carpal tunnel syndrome (Surgical interventions review, Section Introduction and background). Surgery cuts the transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum) to relieve pressure on the nerve and can be done by open, endoscopic or ultrasound-guided methods (Surgical interventions review, Section Different approaches to surgical intervention). A 2018 meta-analysis found surgery gave better symptom relief than conservative treatment after 6 months, with a symptom severity score 0.52 points lower on a 5-point scale (95% CI 0.27 to 0.78) (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention). Prolonged compression can cause permanent nerve damage with wasting of the thenar muscles, which is why severe disease should not be left to long conservative treatment (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?). Risk factors include diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and aromatase inhibitors; in a Saudi survey in Tabuk, chronic disease raised the odds of carpal tunnel syndrome 6.37-fold (adjusted odds ratio, 95% CI 2.05 to 19.82) (Tabuk study, Section Abstract).

symptoms: Numbness, tingling and pain in the hand, often at night, with reduced hand function (Surgical interventions review, Section Abstract; Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).
Persistent symptoms despite at least several months of splinting, injection or other conservative treatment (Kanpur open release study, Section Materials and methods).
Weak grip, dropping objects, clumsiness with fine tasks (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).
physicalSigns: Thenar muscle wasting or weakness of thumb abduction suggests severe disease (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).
Constant numbness or reduced sensation in the median nerve area (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).
Provocation tests are imperfect: Tinel sensitivity 55% and specificity 75%, Phalen 68% and 71%, Durkan 62% and 77%, hand elevation test 85% and 95% (Surgical interventions review, Table 1).
redFlags: Thenar wasting, weakness of the thumb or constant sensory loss: severe disease; arrange nerve conduction studies and urgent referral to a hand or orthopaedic surgeon (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention; Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What to do in Case of an Uncertain Diagnosis or Severe CTS?).
Motor distal latency over 4.5 ms with absent sensory response: severe grade with better response to surgery (Surgical interventions review, Table 2).

Uncertain diagnosis or symptoms beyond the median nerve area: do not operate before investigating other causes such as cervical spine disease (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).

After surgery: increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever at the wound; new loss of thumb movement or new numbness: same-day surgical review (Surgical interventions review, Section Safety evaluation of different surgical interventions).

Symptoms that return after a period of relief: reassess for recurrence or incomplete release; revision was needed in 0.71% after open and 2.08% after endoscopic release in a cohort of 4,338 (Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).
precipitants: Diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, wrist trauma and aromatase inhibitor use (Long-term outcomes study, Section Introduction).
Chronic disease: adjusted odds ratio 6.37 in Tabuk (Tabuk study, Section Abstract).
Factors linked to revision surgery: male sex, tobacco use, concurrent cubital tunnel syndrome and diabetes (Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).
Older age at surgery and current unemployment were linked to poorer long-term outcome (Long-term outcomes study, Section Abstract).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Neck pain and symptoms reproduced by neck movement, spread beyond the median nerve area (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).

differentials.condition: Ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow or wrist
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Little and ring finger numbness; concurrent cubital tunnel syndrome is also a factor in revision surgery (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?; Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).
Glove-and-stocking pattern with abnormal glucose or thyroid tests (Tabuk study, Section Abstract).

differentials.condition: Recurrent or persistent carpal tunnel syndrome after surgery
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Return or persistence of the same symptoms after release; revision rates 0.71% after open and 2.08% after endoscopic release (Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).
Symptoms with arm elevation, or pain on resisted wrist movement without night paraesthesia (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?).

ruleIn.targetCondition: Median nerve slowing at the wrist, graded by Bland criteria

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Used to diagnose, identify severity and follow progress after surgery (Surgical interventions review, Section Introduction and background); sensitivity 87% and specificity 27% (Surgical interventions review, Table 1).
ruleIn.normalValue: Normal median nerve conduction per laboratory reference range

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis and the indication
actions: Check for night numbness, thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction and sensory loss in the median nerve area (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).

Exclude other causes (neck, elbow, thoracic outlet, peripheral neuropathy) and test glucose and thyroid function (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What You Should Do?; Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What are the Known Risk Factors?).
Arrange nerve conduction studies for severe, uncertain or persistent disease (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section What to do in Case of an Uncertain Diagnosis or Severe CTS?).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer for surgical release
actions: Refer to a hand or orthopaedic surgeon when conservative treatment has failed or the disease is severe (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).
Refer urgently when there is thenar wasting, weakness or constant numbness (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Is Physical Examination Sufficient to Initiate Treatment for CTS?).
Treat a causative factor first where one exists, such as hypothyroidism or pregnancy (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).

clinicalManagement.title: Counsel and choose the technique
actions: Explain that surgery gives better symptom and function results than continued conservative treatment after 6 months (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).

Offer open release (clear view of the nerve) or endoscopic release (faster return to activity, more transient nerve injury), chosen by surgeon experience and patient factors (Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).

Record risks: scar tenderness, pillar pain, transient numbness, nerve injury, recurrence and the need for revision (Surgical interventions review, Section Safety evaluation of different surgical interventions).
Record baseline Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire and pain score (Kanpur open release study, Section Materials and methods).

clinicalManagement.title: Perform the release under local anaesthesia
actions: Open release under local anaesthesia was used in the Kanpur cohort; the mean return to work was 11.2 days (Kanpur open release study, Section Results).
Infiltrate local anaesthetic at the lowest dose that gives effective anaesthesia, aspirating before injecting (Xylocaine label, Precautions) (see medicines).
Divide the transverse carpal ligament completely, protecting the median nerve, its recurrent motor branch and the palmar cutaneous branch (Surgical interventions review, Section Open approaches).
Close the wound and apply a dressing (Surgical interventions review, Section Open approaches).

clinicalManagement.title: Give post-operative care
actions: Give simple pain relief and encourage early finger movement (Surgical interventions review, Section Abstract; Surgical interventions review, Section Safety evaluation of different surgical interventions).
Orthoses, dressings, exercise and ice have only minimal, low-quality evidence; use them by surgeon preference (Surgical interventions review, Section Abstract).
Advise avoiding a firm grip for 6 weeks (Frontiers in Medicine 2015 review, Section Surgical decompression (patient information)).

Opioid use was similar after open and endoscopic release in 1,125 patients; plan pain control without relying on opioids (Surgical interventions review, Section Safety evaluation of different surgical interventions).

clinicalManagement.title: Watch for complications
actions: Look for wound infection, hypertrophic or painful scar, pillar pain, numbness or tingling, and reflex sympathetic dystrophy (Surgical interventions review, Section Safety evaluation of different surgical interventions).
Review new thumb weakness or loss of sensation urgently for nerve injury (Surgical interventions review, Section Open approaches).

clinicalManagement.title: Review outcomes
actions: Repeat pain score and Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire at 6 weeks (Kanpur open release study, Section Materials and methods).
In a long-term cohort 73.1% reported complete resolution after an average of 11 years; older age and unemployment predicted poorer outcome (Long-term outcomes study, Section Abstract).
Consider recurrence or incomplete release if symptoms return, and refer back to the surgeon (Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).

regimens.indication: Local anaesthesia for carpal tunnel release
regimens.patientGroup: Adults having open carpal tunnel release under local anaesthesia
regimens.dose: 1% solution (10 mg per mL) infiltrated at the operative site; use the lowest concentration and smallest volume that gives effective anaesthesia, reduced in elderly, debilitated patients and those with cardiac or liver disease (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration). The surgeon decides the volume; the label's maximum dose must not be exceeded. Dilution and preparation: none; use the 1% single-dose solution as supplied and do not use solutions containing preservative for epidural or spinal use.
regimens.route: Local infiltration by percutaneous injection at the wrist and palm; aspirate before and during injection to avoid intravascular injection (Xylocaine label, Precautions)
regimens.frequency: Single administration before incision, with supplemental infiltration only if needed within the label maximum
adjustments: Reduce dose in children, elderly, debilitated patients and patients with cardiac and/or liver disease (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration).
Use with caution in severe hepatic disease because amide anaesthetics are metabolised by the liver (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Solutions containing epinephrine must not be used for intravenous regional anaesthesia and need caution in areas with end arteries or compromised blood supply (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Cardiovascular and respiratory signs and consciousness after each injection; restlessness, anxiety, tinnitus, dizziness, blurred vision or tremor are early warning of toxicity (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Resuscitation equipment and oxygen available (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Allergic reactions: urticaria, oedema, anaphylactoid reaction (Xylocaine label, Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anaesthetics (Xylocaine label, Contraindications).

regimens.indication: Pain after carpal tunnel release, first-line paracetamol
regimens.dose: 2 tablets (1000 mg) per dose (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Directions). Dilution and preparation: none; swallow whole with water.
regimens.frequency: Every 6 hours while symptoms last; no more than 6 tablets (3000 mg) in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Directions)
regimens.duration: Short course; do not use for more than 10 days unless directed by a doctor (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Directions)
adjustments: Liver disease: ask a doctor before use (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Warnings).
Do not combine with another acetaminophen-containing product (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Do not use).
Warfarin: ask a doctor or pharmacist before use (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Warnings).
Pregnancy or breast-feeding: ask a health professional before use (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Warnings).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Total acetaminophen in 24 hours and alcohol intake of 3 or more drinks a day, which raises liver risk (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Warnings).
Pain that worsens or lasts more than 10 days, redness or swelling: review (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Stop using and ask a doctor).
contraindications: Use with any other drug containing acetaminophen (Acetaminophen 500 mg label, Do not use).

regimens.indication: Pain after carpal tunnel release, added to paracetamol if pain is not controlled
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after carpal tunnel release with no contraindication to an anti-inflammatory
regimens.dose: 400 mg per dose (Ibuprofen label, Dosage and Administration); doses above 400 mg were no more effective for pain. Dilution and preparation: none; swallow whole with water and with meals or milk if the stomach is upset.
regimens.frequency: Every 4 to 6 hours as necessary for relief of pain; do not exceed 3200 mg total daily dose (Ibuprofen label, Dosage and Administration)
regimens.duration: Lowest effective dose for the shortest time, guided by the surgeon (Ibuprofen label, Dosage and Administration)
adjustments: Elderly: higher risk of serious gastrointestinal events (Ibuprofen label, Boxed Warning).
Hypertension and heart failure: NSAIDs can worsen both; avoid in severe heart failure (Ibuprofen label, Warnings).
Advanced renal disease: use not recommended (Ibuprofen label, Warnings).
Pregnancy at about 20 weeks or later: risk of fetal renal dysfunction; avoid at about 30 weeks and later (Ibuprofen label, Warnings).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of gastrointestinal bleeding: black stools, vomiting blood, persistent stomach pain (Ibuprofen label, Boxed Warning).
Blood pressure and fluid retention if used for more than a few days (Ibuprofen label, Warnings).
Skin reactions: stop if rash appears (Ibuprofen label, Warnings).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to ibuprofen (Ibuprofen label, Contraindications).
Asthma, urticaria or allergic-type reaction after aspirin or other NSAIDs (Ibuprofen label, Contraindications).
Setting of coronary artery bypass graft surgery (Ibuprofen label, Contraindications).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Failure of conservative treatment, or severe disease with hand numbness, thenar atrophy or reduced hand activity (Surgical interventions review, Section Indications of surgical intervention).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Duration of conservative treatment before surgery in the Kanpur cohort
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: At least 6 months without relief (Kanpur open release study, Section Materials and methods).

Grade 4: motor terminal latency over 4.5 ms and under 6.5 ms with absent sensory potential; grade 5: over 6.5 ms; grade 6: motor potential from abductor pollicis brevis under 0.2 mV (Surgical interventions review, Table 2).

Open, endoscopic or ultrasound-guided release by surgeon experience and patient factors; endoscopic release returns patients to daily activity about 10 days sooner (mean difference -9.56 days, 95% CI -12.51 to -6.60) but has more transient nerve injury (Surgical interventions review, Section Comparison between different surgical techniques).
Return to work mean 11.2 days after open release; pain score fell from 7.4 to 1.5 on a visual analogue scale at 6 weeks (Kanpur open release study, Section Results).

teaching.scope: Adult with carpal tunnel syndrome seen in a Saudi primary health centre, hospital clinic or hand or orthopaedic service: when to refer for surgical release, what to arrange before surgery, the choice between open and endoscopic release, local anaesthesia and simple pain control, wound and hand care afterwards, expected recovery, complications and when to review. learningObjectives: Refer for release when conservative treatment has failed or disease is severe.
Choose open or endoscopic release by surgeon experience and patient factors.
Use simple analgesia and expect return to work in about 2 weeks.
Know the complications and when recurrence needs review.
pitfalls: Operating without excluding neck or other nerve causes.
Giving opioids by default after release.
keyPoints: Thenar wasting means urgent referral, not more splinting.
Endoscopic release recovers sooner but has more transient nerve injury.
Evidence for post-operative splints, dressings and ice is low quality.
Symptoms returning after surgery need reassessment for recurrence.

patientEducation: Surgery cuts the tight band over the nerve at the wrist to relieve pressure; it is usually a day-case operation under local anaesthetic.
Most people feel much better; in one study 94% improved and in another 73% had no symptoms after 11 years.
Move your fingers early after surgery and avoid a firm grip for about 6 weeks.
Many people return to work in about 2 weeks; heavy manual work may take longer.
Contact the surgical team the same day for redness, swelling, discharge, fever, or new weakness or numbness in the thumb.
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce repeated strong gripping and use of vibrating tools where possible.
Take regular breaks from phone and keyboard use.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; hand or orthopaedic surgeon; anaesthetist or nurse for local anaesthesia; neurophysiologist for nerve conduction studies; nurse for wound care; physiotherapist or occupational therapist if stiffness or weakness persists.
dischargeCriteria: Wound care and dressing instructions; analgesia and maximum daily doses; grip and work restrictions (firm grip avoided for 6 weeks); review at 2 and 6 weeks; warning signs requiring same-day review.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at about 2 weeks for the wound and at 6 weeks with pain score and Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire; refer back to the surgeon for recurrent or persistent symptoms.
